findings.title: Lost condvar/join notification to a sleeper embedded in an interrupted process
findings.summary: try_wakeup (manager/mod.rs:1880-1936) scans only the suspended and ready process lists, never the interrupted list. When AlarmFire parks a sleeper inside an interrupted process, a subsequent condvar/join notify pops that waiter off the FIFO (Condvar::notify_first) but try_wakeup_thread cannot find it, so do_wakeup returns NoSuchEntry. The notification is consumed while the still-sleeping thread is never woken (an untimed waiter is stranded forever).
findings.dedup_note: Covers the lost-wakeup half of code-review Scenario 1 (incomplete blocked-thread search set: try_wakeup omits the interrupted list). MC-2 covers the undelivered-signal half of the same Scenario 1 mechanism.

findings.title: Caught signal never delivered to a sleeper in a non-suspended process
findings.summary: interrupt_signal_candidate (manager/mod.rs:1009-1018) resolves a signal candidate only from self.suspended. When kill() posts a caught (handler) signal whose sole unmasked eligible thread is a sleeper embedded in a runnable or interrupted process, no candidate is found and no thread is interrupted, so the signal is never delivered until the process makes an unrelated kernel call.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the undelivered-signal half of code-review Scenario 1 (interrupt_signal_candidate / async delivery scan only a subset of process lists). MC-1 covers the lost-wakeup half of the same Scenario 1 mechanism.

findings.title: Terminated/exited process resumes user code on a carried-forward interrupted thread
findings.summary: RunnableProcess::terminate (runnable.rs:165-203) take()s self.interrupted_threads and re-attaches them unchanged, keeping their TimedOut/Signaled reason; RunningProcess::exit does the same. Only InterruptedProcess::terminate (interrupted.rs:110-125) force-marks interrupted threads Killed. When such a thread is later resumed, ProcessManager::sleep (unsafe.rs:864-869) returns Interrupted(TimedOut) which kcall/sleep.rs:64 maps to Ok(()) (and Signaled to EINTR), so the thread returns to user code even though its process was terminated.
findings.dedup_note: Covers code-review Scenario 2 (terminate/exit does not force-kill already-interrupted threads; only InterruptedProcess::terminate re-marks Killed, the Runnable-terminate and process-exit paths carry TimedOut/Signaled forward).

findings.title: Kernel panic: do_exit dereferences the emptied running slot during rendezvous cleanup
findings.summary: do_exit (manager/mod.rs:2103) calls take_running() (:2116) which sets self.running = None, then cleanup_rendezvous (:2130) wakes each orphaned rendezvous counterpart via do_wakeup -> try_wakeup_thread -> get_running(). get_running (:2785-2787) is self.running.as_ref().expect(...), which panics because running is None. Reachable whenever a thread in another process is blocked as a rendezvous counterpart on the exiting process; a reachable kernel panic / DoS. terminate() is safe because it never nulls running.
findings.dedup_note: Covers code-review Scenario 3 (running==None reentrancy in do_exit: take_running nulls the slot before cleanup_rendezvous' wakeup path unwraps it, panicking).

findings.title: Spurious OutOfMemory: process admission rejected before reclaimable zombies are reaped
findings.summary: create_process (manager/mod.rs:1129) checks self.live_count >= MAX_PROCESSES and returns OutOfMemory at :1139-1147 before any zombie harvest; live_count only decreases at burial (pop_zombie_process, :2458). Unlike the thread-cap path (fix #2495 uses try_next_tid_reaping), the process-cap gate and do_execv's thread reservation lack reap-then-retry, so admission fails spuriously while a reclaimable zombie awaits reaping.
findings.dedup_note: Covers code-review Scenario 4 (reclaimable slots not reaped before cap rejection; the #2495 reap-then-retry fix was not applied to the process-cap gate or do_execv's thread reservation).

findings.title: cond_wait returns EINTR without re-holding the mutex
findings.summary: wait_cond releases the mutex at take_mutex_guard (wait_cond.rs:105) and, after the wait, reacquires with `let guard = mutex.lock(None)?;` (:127). The ? propagates an interrupt and returns without the mutex held; put_cond(...)? (:123) can likewise early-return before the reacquire. POSIX requires pthread_cond_wait to return with the mutex locked even on error, so the caller resumes its critical section without the lock.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the mutex-ownership half of code-review Scenario 5 (blocking-sync cancellation half-releases ownership: interrupted cond_wait reacquire returns without the mutex held). MC-7 covers the slot-conservation half of the same Scenario 5 mechanism.

findings.title: Orphaned mutex-map slot after an interrupted cond_wait reacquire
findings.summary: The only mutex-map reclaimer is put_mutex (state/mod.rs:652-666), reached from a successful unlock. When wait_cond's reacquire is interrupted (MC-6) the caller does not hold the guard, so its later unlock_mutex is rejected as a foreign unlock and never calls put_mutex; the map entry lingers (mutexInMap stays TRUE while unlocked/unowned/unheld), counting against MUTEX_OPEN_MAX until the process exits. lock_mutex cancellation (lock_mutex.rs) is the analogous site (get_mutex created the entry, a timed-out mutex.lock(timeout)? returns before put_mutex) but needs a contended lock (two threads) that scenario5 cannot set up.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the slot-conservation half of code-review Scenario 5 (interrupted/timed-out sync cancellation leaks a mutex-map entry). MC-6 covers the mutex-ownership half. NOTE: Scenario 5's separate 'thread exits while holding a mutex delays sibling wakeup until harvest' sub-claim is NOT covered by any MC candidate and is emitted as CR-4.

findings.title: Blockable default-Terminate signal ignores the per-thread mask
findings.summary: kill() (manager/mod.rs:810) maps a Default disposition whose default_action is Terminate/Core to PostAction::Terminate (:858-866) and calls kill_terminate unconditionally (:892-893) with no per-thread blocked-mask check. Only the Handler path posts to pending (later mask-gated). SIGKILL is handled separately at :842, so ordinary blockable signals with a fatal default action still terminate a target that has the signal masked on every thread, contrary to POSIX (a blocked terminate-default signal should remain pending).
findings.dedup_note: Covers the mask-bypass half of code-review Scenario 6 (signal pending/mask/disposition/lifecycle consistency). MC-9 covers the immortal-pending half. NOTE: Scenario 6's other sub-claims (execv zeroes the pending set -> CR-2; async signal dropped when no restorer + sigsuspend mask leak -> CR-3; no timer-return delivery checkpoint -> CR-5) are NOT covered by any MC candidate and are emitted as CR candidates.

findings.title: Immortal pending signal after a disposition change
findings.summary: sigaction (manager/mod.rs:583-605) calls SignalControl::set_disposition (:605), and set_disposition (state/signal.rs:364-370) only replaces the disposition slot; it never clears a pending instance. try_deliver_signal (manager/signal.rs:243-254) delivers only Handler dispositions and leaves others pending. A signal posted while caught, then re-dispositioned to Default/Ignore, is thus neither delivered nor discarded (stuck pending forever), contrary to POSIX SIG_IGN pending-discard semantics.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the immortal-pending half of code-review Scenario 6 (disposition change to SIG_DFL/SIG_IGN neither delivers nor discards an already-pending signal). MC-8 covers the mask-bypass half of the same Scenario 6 mechanism.

findings.title: Nested sigsuspend overwrites the single saved-mask slot
findings.summary: install_sigsuspend_mask (manager/mod.rs:722-749) unconditionally state.set_saved_blocked(Some(previous)) (:734) into ThreadState.saved_blocked, a single Option<u64> (thread/state.rs:105). A nested sigsuspend (from a handler running before the outer sigreturn) overwrites the outer saved mask, so the outer sigreturn later restores the wrong pre-suspend mask. A single slot cannot represent two nested in-flight signal/sigsuspend contexts.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the saved-mask half of code-review Scenario 7 (sigsuspend/sigreturn/SA_RESTART reentrancy corruption; single-slot saved_blocked cannot hold nested contexts). MC-10b covers the SA_RESTART-attribution half of the same Scenario 7 mechanism.

findings.title: SA_RESTART applied per the delivered signal, not the interrupting one
findings.summary: try_deliver_signal (manager/signal.rs:206-316) consumes the restart record via take_restart() (:220), whose KcallRestart carries the interrupted call's number/args but no signal number. It selects the lowest deliverable caught signal (:240-254) and applies SA_RESTART based on that signal's sa_flags (:280-283), regardless of whether it is the signal that actually interrupted the call. A call interrupted by a non-SA_RESTART signal can thus be transparently restarted (or vice versa) when a different signal is delivered first.
findings.dedup_note: Covers the SA_RESTART-attribution half of code-review Scenario 7 (KcallRestart is signum-less, so restart uses the delivered signal's flags rather than the interrupting signal's). MC-10a covers the saved-mask half of the same Scenario 7 mechanism.

findings.title: join_thread reaps the zombie before copying exit status, losing it on a bad retval pointer
findings.summary: join_thread (kcall/join_thread.rs:70-75) reaps the target thread's zombie slot before copying the exit status out to the caller-supplied retval pointer. If that pointer is invalid, the copy-out fails after the slot has already been reaped, so the exit status is permanently lost and the join cannot be retried. POSIX pthread_join semantics require the status to remain retrievable until a successful join, and the slot should not be consumed on a failed copy. This is a code-review/test-verifiable claim from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: execv clears the process pending-signal set instead of preserving it
findings.summary: reset_for_exec zeroes the process pending-signal set during execv (state/signal.rs:490-497). POSIX requires exec to preserve the set of pending signals (only signal dispositions with handlers are reset to default), so a signal posted and blocked before execv is silently discarded across the image replacement. A thread relying on a queued signal surviving exec would therefore miss it. This is a code-review/test-verifiable claim from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: Async caught signal dropped when no restorer is installed; sigsuspend temp mask leaks
findings.summary: When a caught (handler) signal is delivered asynchronously but no signal restorer/trampoline has been installed, delivery drops the signal instead of terminating the target or surfacing an error (manager/signal.rs:257-268), and any temporary mask installed for a sigsuspend delivery is leaked rather than restored. The result is a silently lost fatal signal plus a corrupted per-thread blocked mask. This deviates from POSIX delivery semantics and can strand a thread with the wrong mask. This is a code-review/test-verifiable claim from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: Thread exiting while holding a mutex blocks a sibling until zombie harvest
findings.summary: A thread that exits while still holding a mutex moves the guard into its zombie thread object (thread/running.rs:195-197); the unlock and Condvar::notify_first that would release a waiting sibling only fire later when the zombie is harvested, and ThreadState::drop merely logs (thread/state.rs:524-533). A sibling blocked on that mutex therefore cannot make progress until zombie harvest runs, a liveness / priority-inversion hazard. POSIX robust-mutex / owner-death handling would expect waiters to be released promptly. This is a code-review/test-verifiable claim from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; it is a distinct mechanism from the cancellation half-release covered by MC-6/MC-7. Confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: CPU-bound thread never receives a caught signal because delivery is kcall-return only
findings.summary: Signal delivery happens only at the kcall-return checkpoint; there is no timer-interrupt-return delivery checkpoint (kcall/dispatcher.rs:240, process/manager/unsafe.rs:899-909). A CPU-bound thread in a tight loop that never issues a kernel call therefore never observes a caught signal posted to it, so kill() with a handler can be indefinitely delayed for that thread. This is either a real delivery-latency/starvation bug or a documented design limitation. This is a code-review/test-verifiable claim from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug or an accepted limitation.

findings.title: post_message/recv can lose a message on error (mutate-then-count / consume-then-copy)
findings.summary: The IPC post_message path (process/manager/mod.rs:3787) mutates queue state before validating/counting, and recv (ipc/recv.rs:56) consumes a message before copying it to the caller's buffer; on an overflow or bad-buffer error the accounting and the message itself can be lost without restoring the queue. This is a mutate-then-count / consume-then-copy ordering hazard that can drop an in-flight message. IPC is only in scope here as a PM precondition, but the loss is flagged in the modeling brief as test-verifiable and was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: capctl performs no privilege check: any process can self-grant any capability
findings.summary: do_capctl (kcall/capctl.rs:32) carries a FIXME and performs no privilege check before changing a process's capabilities, so any process can grant itself any capability, bypassing the capability model (#1434). Other privileged kcalls such as terminate gate on a capability (terminate.rs:49-56); capctl does not. This is a privilege-escalation / security defect. This is a code-review-only finding from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug and whether it is already tracked.

findings.title: duplicate/fork gives the child default capabilities instead of inheriting the parent's
findings.summary: When a process is duplicated/forked, the child is constructed with Capabilities::default() (process/state/mod.rs:253, reached via duplicate_process at manager/mod.rs:1485) rather than inheriting the parent's capabilities, unlike inherited signal state. This may be intended fork policy or an accidental capability drop; it is unconfirmed and undocumented. This is a code-review-only finding from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether the non-inheritance is a bug or the intended policy.

findings.title: CondvarInner::drop panics on a non-empty waiter queue
findings.summary: CondvarInner::drop (sync/condvar.rs:286-291) panics if its waiter queue is non-empty, whereas ThreadState::drop only logs. If a condition variable is ever destroyed while a waiter is still enqueued (for example during process teardown or an error/rollback path), this converts a state inconsistency into a hard kernel panic / DoS. The destructor should either be non-panicking or an assert-unreachable with justification. This is a code-review-only finding from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether the panic is reachable.

findings.title: mmio_alloc skips dry-run/rollback and mmio_free drops ownership without revoking PTEs
findings.summary: The release-only mmio_alloc path (process/manager/mod.rs:3632) skips the two-pass dry-run/rollback that the debug path uses, so a partially completed mapping is not recorded and cannot be cleanly rolled back on failure; mmio_free (:3689) drops ownership without revoking the underlying PTEs. This can leave stale mappings or partially applied address-space changes on the mmap/munmap-adjacent rollback paths. It is relevant to the in-scope address-space-change rollback question. This is a code-review-only finding from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should decide whether it is a real bug.

findings.title: on_thread_reaped relies on a runtime assert to catch live_count underflow
findings.summary: on_thread_reaped (thread/mod.rs:272-281) uses a runtime assert! (thread/mod.rs:277) to guard against live_count underflow, hardening against an accounting bug rather than proving reap paths are balanced. If any reap path (harvest_zombies, reap_deferred, reap_deferred_zombie_threads) is unbalanced, the assert converts the accounting error into a kernel panic instead of a wraparound that breaks admission control. This is a code-review-only / defensive-coding finding from the modeling brief that was never model-checked; confirmation should verify every reap path is balanced so the guard can never fire.
